newsitem.title: GERMANY: CompuServe just first case in German cyber-crusade.
newsitem.headline: CompuServe just first case in German cyber-crusade.

text.p: More criminal charges against online service providers are expected in Germany following the indictment of the head of a unit of CompuServe Inc. for allegedly aiding the dissemination of pornography, lawyers and industry experts said Thursday.

While censorship of Internet providers is commonplace in countries such as China and Singapore, Germany appears to be the first Western democracy to indict an official of an online service for Internet content considered illegal.
The move by prosecutors in the German state of Bavaria Wednesday marked a decisive turning point in the debate over Internet regulation by government authorities.

Just as the German parliament is set to begin debating legislation that takes a liberal view of policing cyberspace, local prosecutors appear to be using CompuServe to set an example meant to urge lawmakers to take a harder line.

"There is hardly an online service or Internet service provider in Germany today that has not been the subject of a criminal investigation," said Michael Schneider, an attorney who specialises in computer law.
"Now that these charges have been raised, I presume others will follow. CompuServe will not be the last case."

In the case of CompuServe, prosecutors indicted Felix Somm, head of its German and Central European operations, for allegedly aiding in the trafficking of child pornography and the dissemination of Nazi symbols and violent computer games that are illegal in Germany.
"CompuServe Inc. considers the charges against Mr. Somm to be baseless and expects that in the end there will be no conviction," the company, which is based in Columbus, Ohio, said in a statement.

The case marks the culmination of police activities over the past year that included raids on the offices of online services as investigators sought to determine who should be held responsible for crimes committed online.

After investigations against CompuServe began in 1995, the company took the unprecedented step of banning access to millions of its members worldwide to over 200 newsgroups, or Internet discussion groups.

The move caused an outcry among CompuServe users and cyber-rights groups in the United States, who were outraged that German authorities could exercise such influence over what Americans were able to read and view online.
German police have teams of cybersleuths looking for evidence of Internet crime, especially child sex rings and extremist literature, such as neo-Nazi writings.
The online industry argues that providers should be viewed merely as telecommunications carriers, rather than publishers who are liable for what is printed in their publications.

"No one would ever bring charges against (phone company) Deutsche Telekom for crimes committed over the telephone," said Schneider. "The problem is that it is not clearly defined how far the responsibility of service providers goes."
America Online Inc.'s German subsidiary, AOL Deutschland, was investigated by Hamburg authorities last year, but no charges were filed.

The Deutsche Forschungsnetz, a scientific research network that offers public Internet access, has been forced to block access to a Dutch site on the World Wide Web that hosted a banned magazine, Radikal.
Germany's largest Internet service provider, EUnet Deutschland GmbH, said German authorities were clearly stepping up Internet investigations.

While German online services and internet access providers are making an effort to cooperate with authorities, they remain convinced that they cannot control cyberspace and should not be held responsible for illicit Web sites.
"We can take responsibility for the content that we produce ourselves but not for that which can be found on the World Wide Web or in newsgroups," AOL spokesman Ingo Reese said.

Germany's draft Information and Communications Services Bill, which comes up for debate in parliament Friday, states that Internet service providers should not be made generally responsible for content on the Internet.

It is one of the first efforts in Europe to define Internet regulation and events in Germany are being watched closely by the European Commission, which has yet to draft any European directive on the issue of Internet regulation.
